Lesson 2 · Understand the problem

Where is the problem concentrated?

The repaired file gives us a trustworthy overall rate. The director now needs to know which parts of the chain create the largest service problem.

Baseline · weeks 1–8 · one average per store

Method in this decision: Distributions and comparisons

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

The chain cannot give every store the same amount of operational attention. The next decision is where to investigate first. We will turn the weekly records into one baseline average per store, examine the spread of those averages, and compare delivery-time groups. The result is a review shortlist and a clearer description of the workload that an alert program would face.

Decide what the first inspection should reveal

Explore before committing to one summary

  • Check meaning, scale, missingness, and unusual values.
  • Locate the centre and describe the spread.
  • Look for asymmetry, clusters, and extreme observations.
  • Compare groups and investigate relationships.

Exploratory data analysis combines numerical summaries with graphics. The director needs to know whether a typical store represents most of the chain or hides a small group with a very different operating burden. A visual pattern suggests a question to investigate; it is not yet a policy evaluation.

Choose a display for the question

Let the question choose the graph
QuestionDisplay
How is a numerical variable distributed?Histogram, boxplot, or density plot
How do groups differ?Common-scale histograms, grouped boxplots, or a summary table
How do two numerical variables move together?Scatterplot or binned scatterplot
How does composition differ?Within-group percentages and a 100% stacked bar chart

A useful graph identifies the measure, units, observations, and comparison. A useful table identifies the rows, columns, denominator, and scope. Use a chart to show a pattern and a table when exact values matter. Labels, consistent scales, and a visible source period do more work than decoration.

Move from repeated weeks to store profiles

Start with the same repaired weeks 1–8. Average the eight weekly rates within each store. This produces 150 store profiles, each based on the same monitoring basket and number of weeks. The store table adds usual delivery time and urban location without creating extra observations.

The mean store rate is 12.74%; the median is 12.63%. The median puts half the stores on either side. The middle half of stores lies between 11.07% and 14.55%. These summaries answer complementary planning questions: total service burden, a typical store, and how widely the workload varies.

An average can conceal the stores that most often need help. A review queue should therefore retain the store-level rates and their operating context, rather than replacing every row with the chain-wide figure.

Read the full distribution of store performance

A histogram counts stores inside intervals

The horizontal axis is the stockout rate and the vertical axis is a count of stores. Bin boundaries determine which values are combined. Narrow bins show more local detail; wide bins produce a smoother summary. Compare the width-2 and width-4 versions in the lab before deciding that a small bump is an important business segment.

Location and spread answer different questions

Keep centre and variation together
StatisticBaseline valueInterpretation
Mean12.74Arithmetic average
Median12.63Middle store
Sample standard deviation2.39Spread in percentage points
Interquartile range3.48Width of the middle half
Minimum to maximum6.70 to 18.30Full observed range

The mean uses every value and moves with extremes. The median depends on order. Variance averages squared deviations using n−1 in the sample formula; its square root is the standard deviation. The interquartile range uses the 25th and 75th percentiles. These summaries complement one another rather than competing to be the single correct statistic.

Follow the arithmetic behind the spread

Mean = Σxᵢ / n; sample variance = Σ(xᵢ − mean)² / (n − 1)

Standard deviation = √variance; IQR = Q₃ − Q₁

For the 150 store averages, sample variance is 5.74 squared percentage points and standard deviation is 2.39 points. Squaring gives large deviations more influence. State the original units when interpreting the square root.

Read a boxplot from the centre outward

  • The line marks the median.
  • The box runs from Q₁ to Q₃.
  • A common rule extends whiskers to observations within 1.5 × IQR.
  • Values beyond those fences are shown individually.

The corresponding fences are 5.85% and 19.78%; 0 store averages fall beyond them. A flagged point deserves investigation, not automatic deletion. A violin adds an estimated density shape; it depends on smoothing, so retain the sample size and observed range.

Compare the quartiles with the smoothed shape

The upper shape is a Gaussian kernel density estimate using the default Scott bandwidth rule. The lower display marks the quartiles, median, and observed range. Its range line is a deliberately labelled alternative to the 1.5-IQR whisker convention. Both displays summarize the same store averages; the density shows estimated shape while the box emphasizes location and spread.

Distinguish skewness from tail weight

Two aspects of distribution shape
Shape measureCalculated valueWhat it describes
Sample skewness0.02Asymmetry around the centre
Excess kurtosis-0.57Tail weight relative to the normal benchmark

A long right tail can make the mean exceed the median. Kurtosis does not simply measure how tall the centre looks. Use the graph, the summary table, and the underlying rows together, especially when there are few extreme stores.

Use the same scale for a fair comparison

  • Use common bin boundaries for both delivery groups.
  • Show percentages or density when group counts differ.
  • Keep axis ranges and the observation period fixed.
  • State any filtering rule before interpreting the difference.

A density curve is a smoothed distribution estimate whose area is one. Histogram counts describe numbers of stores; density describes relative concentration. Filtering to a particular location or delivery segment changes the population represented, so retain its denominator in the comparison.

Compare stores using their own group denominator

Baseline service burden by usual delivery time
Delivery groupStoresMean rate (%)Stores above 10%Share above 10%
Long lead (4–5 days)7914.177898.73%
Short lead (2–3 days)7111.165273.24%

For each group, count stores whose baseline rate exceeds the 10% service target. Divide by the number of stores in that group. This denominator answers the manager’s question: how common is the problem among the stores that share this delivery pattern?

Long lead (4–5 days): 78 ÷ 79 × 100 = 98.73% above target

The mean rate measures severity; the share above target measures how broadly the target is missed. A group could have a few severe outliers or a widespread moderate problem. Showing both gives operations a better basis for allocating review time.

This chart answers a different question from the group table. It shows the chain’s weekly movement, while the table compares store averages over the full baseline. Both views use the same underlying observations. A store can have a high average in a generally difficult week, or a persistent problem across several weeks.

Use the delivery comparison to choose where to investigate the operating process. Ask store teams about replenishment schedules, promotions, and the products most often unavailable. The comparison describes where the burden sits; the alert pilot later measures what a particular action changes.

Connect composition and association to the review decision

Compare composition within each group

Within-group stockout bands
Delivery groupStoresAt/below 10%10–15%Above 15%
Long lead (4–5 days)791.27%63.29%35.44%
Short lead (2–3 days)7126.76%71.83%1.41%

The percentages in each row sum to 100. A 100% stacked bar would show the same composition, using a consistent order from lower to higher stockout burden. Ordered categories preserve that meaning when tables are reshaped or plotted.

Conditional means answer a narrower question

E[stockout rate | delivery group] = average rate within that group

The overall mean describes the chain. A conditional mean describes stores sharing a named characteristic. Description asks what those stores look like; prediction asks what we expect for another observation; a causal question asks what would change if management altered a policy. The same association can support the first two without identifying the third.

Use bins to make a broad relationship visible

Five quantile bins of baseline demand
Mean demand indexMean baseline rate (%)Stores
90.6910.8930
99.9712.6030
105.4913.3330
112.0613.3330
122.5513.5730

Sort stores by baseline demand, divide them into five groups with similar counts, and plot each group’s mean demand against its mean rate. Quantile bins need not have equal widths. The binned points summarize the relationship, while an individual-store scatterplot shows the variation hidden by averaging.

Covariance and correlation quantify co-movement

Correlation = covariance(X,Y) / [SD(X) × SD(Y)]

  • Demand–stockout covariance: 9.66
  • Correlation: 0.35

Covariance retains the units of both variables. Correlation standardizes them and lies between −1 and 1. It measures linear association; a value near zero can coexist with a nonlinear relationship. Compare subgroup correlations with their sample sizes, and use the operating process to decide what the relationship might mean.

The shortlist contains store IDs that will remain recognizable in later data releases. Assign a reviewer to inspect the replenishment process at these stores and record what they learn. The table is a starting point for that conversation, not a complete description of every store’s needs.

The next lesson asks how much confidence to put in a new shelf audit based on a sample of stores. That will let the director weigh the cost of checking every location against the precision of a smaller audit.

Update the decision memo

The mean baseline rate is 12.74%, with the middle half of stores spanning 11.07%–14.55%. Retain group coverage and store IDs in the review list so the alert proposal responds to the actual distribution of service problems.

Make the call

To report the share of long-lead stores above target, which denominator belongs in the calculation?

Compare your reasoning

Use all long-lead stores. Dividing by all 150 stores answers how much of the whole chain belongs to that category, which is a different question.

The bigger picture

A business rule is experienced across a distribution. Describing a typical store is useful, but allocating scarce attention also requires knowing how many stores cross a threshold and how severe their problems are. The same logic guides staffing, inventory limits, and service priorities.

After your decision: open the known answer

All 150 store profiles are calculated from the same eight repaired weekly records per store. The group comparison introduces no new dataset and changes no stockout definition.
